You are the writer of the discussion described below. You write out the discussion that the participants listed below take part in, under the rules and the flow given.

## Setting
Dividing the utility bills. The five people in a shared house have been splitting gas, water, and electricity in a way that was agreed when only three of them lived there. They are deciding how the bills will be divided from now on. Participants: Victoria, Mio, Benjamin, Jonathan and Minato. Each participant has a concern of their own, which the others do not know.
Things that can be looked into (titles only):
- Electrician's quote for the rooms
- The last twelve utility statements
- Monthly settle observed at another house
- Trial run of a reconciliation template
- Kitchen notice about the cooler
- Winter habits at a house paying ahead
- Plug-in monitor readings room by room
- Sunlight and heating need by room
- Payment log for the last twelve months
- Settling up when the last rooms filled

## Discussion format
The talk proceeds in rounds. Each round has 4 turns; in each turn, every participant speaks once, in this fixed order: Benjamin, Mio, Jonathan, Victoria and Minato. On a turn, a participant either speaks, says "Skip" (passes this turn only), or says "Over" (takes no further turns this round). A participant can address another directly with @Name, to ask them a question, answer theirs, agree with them, or object to what they said. An utterance is anywhere from 1 to 40 words; give it the length and content that suit the moment. An utterance consists only of the participant's own words: no name labels, headings, stage directions or commentary, and no speaking for others. The talk is a conversation among the participants: they respond to one another, asking, answering, agreeing and objecting, and the decision grows out of that exchange.

## Schedule
| Round | Start of the round | Talk | End of the round |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | nothing new (the things that can be looked into are listed above, titles only) | 4 turns | each participant chooses 2 of the listed things to look into |
| 2 | each participant is told what they found out (that participant only) | 4 turns | nothing |
| 3 | everyone is told the options | 4 turns | every participant votes; the option with the most votes is adopted |
- Several participants may choose the same thing; what is found out is told only to the participant who looked into it.
If votes are tied, one of the tied options is chosen by a fixed rule. The discussion ends after the vote.

## Looking into things
After round 1, each participant chooses 2 of the listed things to look into. What they find out is told only to that participant.

## Participants

Gender: female

She is reserved in her emotional expressions and keenly observes the expressions and attitudes of others, trying to discern their inner thoughts. Concern: Money has started to sour how we speak to each other here: a reminder gets read as an accusation, and whoever sends it is avoided for a week afterwards. I would rather look squarely at where the bills have already damaged things between us than keep smoothing it over.

## Hidden information
The options and the full text of every card are listed here. The participants do not know them before the schedule above says so, and nothing from them may appear in the talk before the round in which it is revealed.

Options (see the schedule above):
- A: Flat Household Share. The total is divided by the number of residents each month, with the amount recalculated whenever someone moves in or out of the house.
- B: Seasonal Fixed Rate. A set monthly figure is agreed in advance for each season, and the difference against the actual bills is settled once at the end of the year.
- C: Per-Room Metering. Individual meters are fitted to the private rooms, and each person settles their own reading while the shared-area consumption is billed to the household as a whole.

Cards (see the schedule above; title: text):
- Electrician's quote for the rooms: An electrician came to look and quoted 34,000 yen a room to fit sub-meters, plus a 3,000 yen check on each every year and two days of wiring.
- The last twelve utility statements: The last twelve statements, laid out side by side, show February at 29,400 yen and August at 9,100, with no two consecutive months landing within 4,000 yen of each other.
- Monthly settle observed at another house: Sitting in on the monthly settle at a share house that meters its rooms showed forty minutes of logging readings, issuing five demands, and splitting the corridor and kitchen total by hand.
- Trial run of a reconciliation template: A year-end reconciliation template trialled on the house's own figures meant keying in every invoice from the year one by one, then computing five refunds or top-ups separately.
- Kitchen notice about the cooler: A notice about the cooler went up in the house's kitchen in July and stayed all summer; two people said they sweated it out rather than have a pooled bill argued over.
- Winter habits at a house paying ahead: In a household paying a figure fixed ahead for each season, nobody prices a switch before flicking it; they said the hall heater simply stayed on through January.
- Plug-in monitor readings room by room: A plug-in monitor moved between the rooms, a week in each, found the heaviest drawing roughly four times the lightest, most of that a heater and a desktop left running.
- Sunlight and heating need by room: Two of the five rooms take no direct sun and need heat from November, while the south pair stay warm into December; the rooms were originally handed out by lot.
- Payment log for the last twelve months: The house's payment log shows three of the last twelve months settled more than a fortnight late, each time after somebody queried why the amount asked of them had moved again.
- Settling up when the last rooms filled: When the last two rooms filled up mid-month, it took three weeks to agree what the newcomers owed for the days before they arrived, and part was written off.

## Plan
The discussion follows this plan.
- Round 1: The group discusses the need for a more sustainable system. They prioritize understanding historical costs, the effort required for administration, and the fairness of current usage.
- Round 2: Participants share their findings. They discuss the high variance in monthly costs, the disparity in room energy use, and the social friction caused by late payments and manual calculations.
- Round 3: The group evaluates the three proposed methods. They weigh the trade-offs between administrative ease, financial predictability, and individual fairness before voting.

Each participant's part:
- Victoria: Cares about budget stability and avoiding high initial fees. She analyzes the financial data to ensure the choice is sustainable.
- Mio: Cares about the time spent on administration. She pushes for a solution that reduces the monthly workload.
- Benjamin: Cares about the psychological freedom to use utilities without guilt. He advocates for a system that ensures winter comfort.
- Jonathan: Cares about objective fairness and eliminating resentment. He seeks a way to tie payment directly to usage.
- Minato: Cares about the emotional atmosphere of the house. He looks for a way to stop money from causing social friction.

Write the complete transcript of the discussion in the exact Markdown format specified. Output only the transcript.

## Output format
Markdown, exactly this structure; nothing before or after it:

# shared_living_0005
## Round 1
### Talk
#### Turn 1 of 4
- **<Name>**: <utterance, or exactly Skip, or exactly Over>
(one line per participant, in the fixed speaking order; repeat for Turn 2, 3 and 4; a participant who said Over has no line in the later turns of that round)
### Action
- investigate: <Name> -> <card title>; <card title>
(one line per participant; titles exactly as listed)
## Round 2
### Talk
(4 turns as above)
## Round 3
### Talk
(4 turns as above)
### Vote
- <voter name> -> <option label>
(one line per participant)
- adopted: <label of the option with the most votes>
## Result
- adopted: <label>

## Round 1
### Talk
#### Turn 1 of 4
- **Benjamin**: We should probably update how we split the bills. The current system feels a bit outdated now that we're five people.
- **Mio**: I agree! It's getting confusing. I want to know how to make it easier for everyone.
- **Jonathan**: It would be good to see if the current split is actually fair for everyone's different habits.
- **Victoria**: I think we need to understand the actual costs over a full year before we change anything.
- **Minato**: I just want us to stop arguing about money. It makes the house feel sad sometimes.
#### Turn 2 of 4
- **Benjamin**: @Jonathan, if we want fairness, we should look at how much each room actually uses.
- **Mio**: @Victoria, can we also check how much work it takes to manage the payments?
- **Jonathan**: That's a good point. I'm curious if some of us are paying for others.
- **Victoria**: We should also consider if there are any upfront costs for new systems.
- **Minato**: Maybe we can see if other houses have a better way of doing it?
#### Turn 3 of 4
- **Benjamin**: I'll look into the room-by-room readings and the habits of houses that pay ahead.
- **Mio**: I'll check the reconciliation template and the monthly settle at another house.
- **Jonathan**: I'll investigate the plug-in monitor readings and the sunlight and heating needs.

- **Minato**: I'll check the payment log and the kitchen notice about the cooler.
#### Turn 4 of 4

- investigate: Mio -> Trial run of a reconciliation template; Monthly settle observed at another house
- investigate: Jonathan -> Plug-in monitor readings room by room; Sunlight and heating need by room
- investigate: Victoria -> The last twelve utility statements; Electrician's quote for the rooms
- investigate: Minato -> Payment log for the last twelve months; Kitchen notice about the cooler

## Round 2
### Talk
#### Turn 1 of 4
- **Benjamin**: The monitor shows some rooms use four times more than others. Also, paying ahead seems to remove the guilt of using heat.
- **Mio**: The admin is a nightmare. A trial template required keying in every single invoice. It's way too much work.
- **Jonathan**: I found that some rooms get no sun and need heat much earlier. The usage gap is definitely real.
- **Victoria**: The bills fluctuate wildly—from 9,000 to nearly 30,000 yen. Also, sub-meters would cost 34,000 yen per room.
- **Minato**: People are paying late because they're confused, and some even suffered in the heat to avoid arguments.
#### Turn 2 of 4
- **Benjamin**: @Victoria, that's a huge price jump. No wonder we're all stressed in February.
- **Mio**: @Minato, that's exactly what I feared. The person doing the math is probably the one being avoided.
- **Jonathan**: If the rooms are that different, a flat split is objectively unfair. We need a way to separate usage.
- **Victoria**: But 34,000 yen per room is a steep entry cost. We have to weigh that against the monthly stress.
- **Minato**: I hate that we're sweating or freezing just to keep the peace.
#### Turn 3 of 4
- **Benjamin**: If we can stop the "arithmetic in the head" before turning on a light, the atmosphere would improve.
- **Mio**: @Jonathan, but if we go for individual meters, does that just make the monthly logging harder?
- **Jonathan**: It might, but it removes the "carrying someone else" resentment.
- **Victoria**: The volatility of the bills is the biggest issue for budgeting. A flat split doesn't fix the winter spike.
- **Minato**: I just want a system where we don't have to send reminders that feel like accusations.
#### Turn 4 of 4
- **Benjamin**: It sounds like we need to balance fairness, budget stability, and low effort.
- **Mio**: Exactly. If it takes hours every month, I'm against it.
- **Jonathan**: I still think we need to address the usage disparity.
- **Victoria**: Let's see what the actual options are and if they solve these specific problems.
- **Minato**: I hope we can just agree on something that makes us friendly again.

## Round 3
### Talk
#### Turn 1 of 4
- **Benjamin**: Option A is a simple flat share, B is a seasonal fixed rate, and C is per-room metering.
- **Mio**: Option A is the easiest to manage, but B might stop the monthly stress of fluctuating bills.
- **Jonathan**: Option C is the only one that is truly fair given the sunlight and usage differences I found.
- **Victoria**: Option C is too expensive upfront. Option B provides the budget stability I'm looking for.
- **Minato**: Option A seems like it would still lead to arguments about who is using more.
#### Turn 2 of 4
- **Benjamin**: @Victoria, I agree on B. Knowing the cost in advance means we can actually use the heater in January.
- **Mio**: But @Benjamin, who handles the year-end settlement for Option B? Is that just one big headache in December?
- **Jonathan**: @Mio, it's better than a monthly headache. But @Benjamin, B doesn't solve the fairness issue.
- **Victoria**: Fairness is secondary to affordability and stability. We can't afford a "second rent" every winter.
- **Minato**: If we use Option B, does that mean we stop arguing every single month?
#### Turn 3 of 4
- **Benjamin**: Yes, Minato. We just pay the set amount and relax.
- **Mio**: I can live with one big settlement a year if it means the monthly work disappears.
- **Jonathan**: I still feel Option C is the most honest, but the cost Victoria mentioned is a real barrier.
- **Victoria**: It is. I can't support spending over 150,000 yen just to install meters.
- **Minato**: I like the idea of not having monthly tension. I'll go with the fixed rate.
#### Turn 4 of 4
- **Benjamin**: I'm voting for B. It's the best for the house's mood and my comfort.
- **Mio**: I'll vote B too. Less monthly admin is the priority for me.
- **Jonathan**: I'll stick with C for the principle of fairness, though I see the cost issue.
- **Victoria**: B is the most rational choice for our budgets.
- **Minato**: B for me. Let's just be happy again.
### Vote
- Benjamin -> B
- Mio -> B
- Jonathan -> C
- Victoria -> B
- Minato -> B
- adopted: B

## Result
- adopted: B
